title: The ADD Instruction
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of the add instruction.
Choose and interpret a suitable Docker example connected to the add instruction.
Predict an expected result and verify it using observable evidence in a controlled environment.

content.intro: This lesson covers The ADD Instruction. You will connect the named subtopics from the supplied Docker curriculum to a small, observable example. Work through the visual first, then use the example to form a prediction and check it against the actual behavior.
content.why_it_matters: A Dockerfile declares how a build should assemble an image. Use an explicit base, predictable paths, a minimal build context, appropriately ordered dependency steps, and a startup command that matches the application. Build-time configuration and runtime configuration have different purposes. Learning the add instruction helps you make deployment behavior explicit and repeatable instead of relying on a command that happened to work on one machine.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with the supplied example for the add instruction. Before running it, state what you expect to happen. Compare the real output with that prediction, then change one variable or setting in a disposable lab to test the boundary of the idea. If a command is not supported on your operating system or installed Docker version, consult the linked official reference and record the actual version rather than guessing.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: The ADD Instruction
content_blocks.code:
# Prefer COPY for ordinary local files.
FROM nginx:alpine
COPY ./site/ /usr/share/nginx/html/

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming that a successful start means the application is ready.
common_mistakes.why: A container can start while its dependent service is unavailable or the application is failing after startup.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect health/status and logs; add a meaningful health check or retry strategy where appropriate.

common_mistakes.problem: Keeping required data only in the container writable layer.
common_mistakes.why: Replacing the container can discard that layer and its application state.
common_mistakes.fix: Select a named volume or an external storage system, then rehearse a restore.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a command without checking context, target, or permissions.
common_mistakes.why: Docker commands affect the active endpoint and can change host resources or publish services.
common_mistakes.fix: Check `docker context show`, use an isolated lab, make the smallest change, and verify the resulting state.
